Determine the radius $r$ of the circular sector with the largest possible area that can be made with a wire that's $40\,\text{cm}$ in length. Do not round the answer.

$r=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{cm}$
question.worked_solution:
First,  let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta $ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. We want to maximize the area

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $40\,\text{cm},$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
40=2r+\theta r.
$$

Now, by making $\theta $ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\theta =\frac{40-2r}{r}=\frac{40}{r}-2.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A(r) & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}(\frac{40}{r}-2) \\  & =20r-{r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{A}^{′}(r)=20-2r.
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ 20-2r & =0 \\ -2r & =-20 \\ r & =\frac{(-20)}{(-2)} \\ r & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=10$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(10)=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(10)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=10$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Therefore, the circular sector with the largest area will be that in which the radius $r$ is equal to $10\,\text{cm}.$
